segments.source: Source 5
segments.context: The five-pound choice should follow the household's real consumption. Roughly 2,268 g at 20 g each day is about 113 days before waste; at 80 g each day it is about 28 days. The same package therefore makes very different demands on two kitchens. Stumptown's opened-bag guidance is a useful reason to make that calculation before treating bulk as a bargain. [5]

segments.source: Source 6
segments.context: A cool, dark location and a well-sealed bag or container are practical starting choices. Stumptown also warns about moisture introduced by repeatedly moving coffee in and out of cold storage and about absorbing surrounding odors. Its advice is cited as guidance, not a blanket experiment on every coffee here. [6]

segments.source: Source 7
segments.context: Baratza's Encore ESP manual offers a useful example for a separate grinder: coffee-oil cleaning is discussed for dark or oily coffee, while metal burrs must stay dry. Its washable removable containers are not permission to wash the burrs. That distinction matters when a coffee purchase changes the cleaning workload. [7]

segments.source: Our reason to shortlist it is practical: a household that already enjoys a familiar coffee can test a modest change without buying the darkest option first. The trial should be against the actual routine. A coffee that works well for a small cappuccino may be less distinctive in a large milky drink, and neither outcome is automatically a failure.

segments.source: Counter Culture presents Big Trouble as a coffee for multiple brewing methods. Its general 1:17 water guidance is a filter-style starting point, not a command to send that amount of water through espresso grounds. Use a method-specific recipe and record the dry coffee and beverage quantities.

segments.source: For espresso, begin with a dose your basket accepts comfortably and your machine's normal repeatable workflow. Keep dose and yield fixed for the first grinder change so that you can identify the effect. A timer helps document that change; it does not determine whether the flavor fits your preference. For filter, keep batch size, paper and agitation comparable before blaming the coffee.

segments.source: If your espresso grinder cannot make a small enough adjustment, switching between several bags may hide the hardware limitation rather than solve it. The Encore ESP's documented adjustment and cleaning routine is a relevant example of the controls and care needed for mixed-method use. It is not evidence that Big Trouble performs best on that grinder.

segments.source: Ask whether the present setup can return to a known recipe after someone makes filter coffee. Mark the setting, weigh the dose and record the yield. If the next espresso needs a large correction, consider retained grounds, a different dose and the changed coffee as separate possibilities. Buying another bag is cheaper than another grinder, but it is still a poor diagnostic method when everything changes together.

segments.source: Keep oil-related grinder care separate from water-path maintenance. A descale operation in the espresso machine cannot clean grounds retained in a separate grinder. Follow each manufacturer's directions for its own appliance, and do not substitute washing metal burrs for dry cleaning.

segments.source: Hologram is a year-round recipe, not a fixed-origin lot. Counter Culture says it combines natural-sundried and washed coffees from long-term partners in Africa and Latin America. The natural components are intended to bring fruit and body; washed components are intended to bring pastry and chocolate. That describes the roaster’s design, not a Coffeedant sensory result.

Match the bag’s roast date to the live selector before treating a breakdown as current. Individual varieties were not specified for the full blend.

segments.source: Counter Culture labels Hologram “fruity,” “milk chocolate” and “syrupy.” The roaster says its team cups coffees and selects the most prominent descriptors; it also says no flavoring agents are added. These are roaster-attributed notes. Coffeedant has not tasted this coffee, scored its acidity or sweetness, or established that every lot has the same intensity.

segments.source: An August 2026 Guardian comparison of eleven Counter Culture coffees identified Hologram’s fruit-and-chocolate character and relayed a home barista’s advice to keep milk drinks relatively small if you want the fruit to remain noticeable. That is an independent tasting context for a particular sample, not proof that a different roast-date bag will taste identical. Owner comments are mixed: some enjoy Hologram for both espresso and pour-over; another recent AeroPress owner struggled to find the advertised notes. These accounts help set expectations, not an average rating or a defect rate.

segments.source: Our buying judgment is therefore about fit: Hologram has a more adventurous flavor brief than a straight caramel-and-nut blend, but the chocolate component gives it a familiar anchor. If any fruit note reads as unwanted sharpness to you, do not assume a finer grind alone will make this the right coffee. Try a smaller bag before committing to 24 oz or 5 lb.

segments.source: Counter Culture markets the blend for various brew methods and suggests grinding immediately before brewing. Its broad starting point is one gram of coffee to seventeen grams of water for most devices. For a 20 g filter dose, that implies about 340 g water; it is a starting ratio, not an exact recipe or quality guarantee. Adjust grind and ratio one variable at a time, using the actual bag and brewer as the final reference.

segments.source: Espresso uses a different ratio and extraction regime, so do not copy the 1:17 filter suggestion into a portafilter. Begin with your machine and basket’s normal dose, record beverage mass and time, taste, and make small grinder changes. Milk can soften fruit and emphasize chocolate, but a large milk drink can also hide the reason you chose Hologram. The Guardian’s smaller-milk suggestion is a useful test, not a rule.

segments.source: For people alternating brew methods, a grinder that can return repeatably to an espresso setting matters more than a bag claiming “all-purpose.” Coffeedant’s grinder guide compares the trade-offs, and its Encore ESP review covers a lower-cost mixed-method route. The coffee cannot compensate for stale grinding, unsuitable water or an unrepeatable recipe.

segments.source: Counter Culture advises checking a “Roasted On” date rather than a best-by date. Its freshness guide recommends keeping whole beans tightly sealed in the original one-way-valve bag with excess air pressed out, or in an airtight container that lets carbon dioxide escape without admitting oxygen. Grind just before brewing. The advice is more useful than a rigid claim that all coffees peak on the same day: roast, packaging, shipping, storage and brewing method differ.

segments.source: A grocery-shelf bag and a direct-order bag can have different histories even when the front label is the same. Check the actual roast date and package condition. If you drink one or two cups daily, start with 12 oz; the 24 oz and 5 lb options make sense only if your household or office will use them while they still meet your preferred flavor standard. Counter Culture specifically advises against refrigerating or freezing opened coffee because it can absorb moisture and odors, and recommends a cool, dry place instead.

segments.source: That price is not a promise about Target, grocery stores or future direct orders. The better value question is whether the bag’s roast date, rotating composition and flavor direction make you likely to finish it. A cheaper older bag can be poor value if you use only half. A larger bag is not automatically economical when it outlasts the freshness you enjoy.
